channel.title: Robotics & AI Daily Briefing
channel.description: New cs.RO and cs.AI papers, bucketed and summarized every arXiv announcement day

item.title: Today's papers find manipulation policies that succeed without doing what was asked or when it was asked: they ignore the instruction, act on state that went stale while people moved, and only benchmarks that score the instruction, the timing and the contact catch it.
item.description:
Today's papers find manipulation policies that succeed without doing what was asked or when it was asked: they ignore the instruction, act on state that went stale while people moved, and only benchmarks that score the instruction, the timing and the contact catch it.
Many of today's papers check whether a robot's success means what it seems to mean, and often it does not. ManipScope finds that ten policy checkpoints follow the reassigned instruction on 3.9% of states, worse than a chooser that ignores language. Two training papers and a VLM safety audit trace the same shortcut to visual priors that crowd out the instruction. New benchmarks add what clean, synchronous success rates leave out: a world that keeps moving during inference, contact with distractors, and the physical act of pressing keys. The human-facing work treats time as the safety variable. A robot agent writes its own interrupt for when a person steps in, a navigation planner puts a deadline on a plan while the LLM is still thinking, and a swarm safety filter breaks once neighbour estimates are older than about 150 ms. For a team building robots that live among people of different ages and cultures, the advice is to test whether the robot followed this person's request, at this moment, and score the contacts it made along the way.

item.title: This week's numbers were less trustworthy than they looked. Success checkers, world-model losses, fluent language and demographic prompts all overstated how well robots work, and the papers that measured people directly found that partners, ages and workload break designs that look finished.
item.description:
This week's numbers were less trustworthy than they looked. Success checkers, world-model losses, fluent language and demographic prompts all overstated how well robots work, and the papers that measured people directly found that partners, ages and workload break designs that look finished.
The week had four snapshots: 16, 18, 19 and 20 November. The theme that recurred most was that the usual number misleads. A learned simulator that predicts better can still produce failing policies. A VLA can pick the right bowl for a synonym and still not finish the task. Benchmark success checkers accept incomplete runs, and most world-model planner failures turn out to be stalls in the planning loop rather than model error. Touch appeared on three days with a consistent rule: it helps when it is registered in the robot frame and gated, not concatenated raw. Post-training kept moving onto the robot's own rollouts, failures and intervention logs. The human-facing papers asked the most of a team building robots for people of different ages and cultures. A handover policy collapsed with unfamiliar partners, task success saturated while workload and acceptance still separated designs, and age-prompted VLMs shifted affect in the opposite direction to real older adults. Single-day themes that did not recur included motor heat as the limit on legged endurance (18 November), arm kinematics as free calibration (19 November) and event-triggered calls to large models (20 November). They are still worth keeping.

item.title: Several of today's papers find that the measuring tools themselves are wrong: benchmark success checkers, physics scores, world-model costs and age or persona prompts report things that are not true. The useful fixes diagnose where the failure is before anyone retrains a model.
item.description:
Several of today's papers find that the measuring tools themselves are wrong: benchmark success checkers, physics scores, world-model costs and age or persona prompts report things that are not true. The useful fixes diagnose where the failure is before anyone retrains a model.
Today's papers share one move: they stop trusting the number and check what produced it. Success checkers in RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365 and RoboDojo accept unfinished executions and reject valid ones. Physics-IQ rewards video models for blurring. A world-model planner's cost can be at chance on predicted outcomes while it is sound on real ones. VLMs told to answer as an older adult move valence in the direction opposite to what older people actually report. The same diagnostic habit shows up at runtime. Planners break stalls instead of adapting weights, large reasoning models are called only when a monitor flags trouble, and safety work measures what the robot physically does after it stops, not only whether the task was completed. For a team building robots for people of many ages and cultures, the most direct lesson is that human-likeness has to be checked against measured human data, item by item, and a demographic prompt does not provide that.

item.title: Several of today's papers show that a robot policy has memorized or only skimmed what looked like competence (camera placement, word meaning, task success). The fixes come from the robot's own kinematics, its own rollouts and progress monitoring, not from more demonstrations.
item.description:
Several of today's papers show that a robot policy has memorized or only skimmed what looked like competence (camera placement, word meaning, task success). The fixes come from the robot's own kinematics, its own rollouts and progress monitoring, not from more demonstrations.
A thread runs through today's listing: what a deployed policy appears to understand is often memorized or surface-level. VLAs fine-tuned on a few demos have memorized the camera-to-base extrinsics, and two independent papers undo a bumped camera by using the arm itself, placed by forward kinematics, as the calibration target. A VLA sends synonyms to the right bowl but fails to finish the task. A VLM judge passes children's illustrations that people flag as culturally wrong. VLM agents state 90% confidence while being right 38.9% of the time. The constructive answers share a pattern. Post-training steers a policy's initial noise or relabels its own rollouts instead of collecting more expert demos. Long-horizon reliability comes from a monitor that tracks progress around a frozen short-horizon VLA. Touch helps once it is placed in the robot frame and gated, not fused raw. For a team building robots for people of many ages and cultures, the human-facing studies add a warning: task success saturates early, and workload, acceptability and response timing are what separate designs.

item.title: Today's most useful papers measure what actually limits a deployed robot (the demo-collection rig, motor heat, the decision a world model drives, the stage where a VLA fails) instead of the proxy metric the field usually reports.
item.description:
Today's most useful papers measure what actually limits a deployed robot (the demo-collection rig, motor heat, the decision a world model drives, the stage where a VLA fails) instead of the proxy metric the field usually reports.
Many of today's papers make the same move: they stop trusting the usual proxy and measure what actually limits deployment. On data, a study drawing on hundreds of thousands of hours shows that teleoperation latency, calibration and operator detours end up in the learned policy. Fast kinesthetic demos and a USD 557 hand-worn rig show that the collection interface sets the policy's ceiling. On world models, an independent audit and a decision-certificate method both show that one-step accuracy and visual plausibility do not predict whether a policy or plan built on the model works. VLA work is moving from one success rate to locating failures in a stage, a workspace region or a visual input. Legged deployments find that motor heat, not battery, ends sustained operation. For a team building robots that interact with people, the human-facing papers point the same way: graded risk around people, listening as well as looking in group conversation, and securing the configuration layer of LLM-driven social robots.

item.title: Robots trained with one partner, one sensor condition or one demo set break on the next one, and today's fixes randomize the hidden variable, gate unreliable perception, and mine the policy's own failures.
item.description:
Robots trained with one partner, one sensor condition or one demo set break on the next one, and today's fixes randomize the hidden variable, gate unreliable perception, and mine the policy's own failures.
The common thread today is what happens when a robot meets something its training did not show it. A self-play handover policy that succeeds 95% of the time with its own partner drops to 31% with unfamiliar ones, and an accessibility benchmark shows VLMs failing to change their path choices across user profiles. On the perception side, navigation and locomotion papers stop assuming the depth or image is right and build explicit fallback, revision and re-check steps. On the learning side, several groups generate post-training data from the states where a VLA or reasoning model fails, mostly in simulation, while controlled single-factor studies (perception noise, cross-view geometry, contact cues) explain why policies are brittle in the first place. For a team building robots that interact with people of different ages and cultures, the practical message is to treat the human partner as a distribution to randomize and test against, the same way perception noise already is.

item.title: This week showed that both simulated humans and benchmark scores flatter robot methods, while the human-facing papers that tested with real people found the gaps sit in per-person differences and nonverbal cues.
item.description:
This week showed that both simulated humans and benchmark scores flatter robot methods, while the human-facing papers that tested with real people found the gaps sit in per-person differences and nonverbal cues.
The week had two snapshots, 9 and 11 November, and both returned to the gap between what a benchmark rewards and what a robot needs among people. On 9 November, simulated intervention and preference models were shown to rank methods differently from real users, and on 11 November a training-free retrieval baseline, clock-indexed memory and auto-exposed cameras explained results that looked like policy capability. General-model agent harnesses beat specialist VLAs on public suites, and the safety work responded by putting gates outside the model rather than in the prompt. Human-facing papers kept finding that people differ, in haptic percepts, affect and social cues, and that home and companion agents fail by over-acting or over-remembering. For a team building robots for people of different ages and cultures, the steady advice is to add shortcut baselines, score prohibited actions as failures, and budget for per-user calibration and participant studies.

item.title: Robot results are increasingly being checked against shortcuts, and the human-facing papers today show that social cues are still where current models fall short.
item.description:
Robot results are increasingly being checked against shortcuts, and the human-facing papers today show that social cues are still where current models fall short.
Several papers today test whether a robot's apparent competence comes from the capability it is supposed to show. A kNN retrieval baseline reaches 91.7% on LIBERO, a memory VLA stops early when a wrist fidget is inserted, and the same policies barely change when room light drops 11.5x, because the cameras auto-expose. In the human-facing work, a humanoid negotiator that updates its affect model online gets higher concession rates from 66 participants, and a social robot with emotion-conditioned gestures is preferred by 60 participants, while a child-centric benchmark shows VLMs collapsing on behavioral and interpersonal cues. On the safety side, the common move is to take the decision out of the model: a lease-style gate on each action, a code-driven workflow instead of an LLM choosing each step, and a barrier steering the latent before a path-space filter. For a team building robots that interact with people of different ages and cultures, the practical message is to evaluate with humans and with shortcut-breaking controls, not with the headline benchmark number alone.

item.title: The human side of robot learning is the bottleneck today: simulated people misjudge methods, home agents over-act, and stated traits predict little.
item.description:
The human side of robot learning is the bottleneck today: simulated people misjudge methods, home agents over-act, and stated traits predict little.
Today's papers point at the same weak link: the human in the loop is modelled, labelled or reported in ways that do not match real people. Q-OIL and Goodhart in the Planner show that simulated interventions and synthetic preference labels change which methods look good and how far a planner can be pushed before the task fails. HomeLoop and Relic show that home and companion agents fail by acting too much and by remembering without governance, and the self-report and tone studies suggest that what a model says about itself or how it sounds is a weak guide to what it will do. On the capability side, agentic harnesses around general models now beat specialist VLAs on public benchmarks, which makes the evaluation question more urgent, not less.

item.title: The week's recurring lesson was that scores can mislead: offline metrics, in-distribution verifiers and nominal benchmarks all rank policies differently from the robot.
item.description:
The week's recurring lesson was that scores can mislead: offline metrics, in-distribution verifiers and nominal benchmarks all rank policies differently from the robot.
Across 2 to 6 November, the papers kept returning to the gap between what a team measures and what the robot or the person experiences. Checkpoint selection by validation loss or pass@1 was shown to rank policies backwards on hardware (2 and 3 November), and verifier-tied benchmark gains were shown to vanish when criteria shifted slightly (6 November). In parallel, latency, tactile and reflex work moved signals into the control loop, and human-facing studies showed that perceived safety, workload and care can move independently of physical or task metrics. Human data was judged by embodiment match rather than volume, and runtime monitors and safety filters began to carry explicit bounds or guarantees. For a ROS 2 team, the consistent response is to test on the robot in closed loop, hold out a verifier or stimulus variant, and record the human-side outcome beside task success.

item.title: Social and safety behaviour is being learned into robot policies, with training-only signals doing much of the work while evaluation lags behind.
item.description:
Social and safety behaviour is being learned into robot policies, with training-only signals doing much of the work while evaluation lags behind.
Today's papers share one shift: the signals that make robots social, safe and cheap to run are increasingly used during training and dropped at deployment. Humanoid papers make partner motion and intent explicit inputs, while VLA papers move foresight and alignment into losses or branches that are removed at inference. The same pattern shows up in runtime monitoring, where failure-mode prediction with bounds replaces a single failure score. The weak link is evaluation: criteria that shift slightly, and self-reported success, can make a result look stronger than the robot's real behaviour. For a team shipping humanoids, the practical work is to instrument intent, latency and held-out verifiers together.

item.title: Robot evaluation is moving past one success score toward human-perceived safety, failure boundaries, and the per-hardware cost of running the policy.
item.description:
Robot evaluation is moving past one success score toward human-perceived safety, failure boundaries, and the per-hardware cost of running the policy.
Several papers today refuse to let one aggregate number stand in for a robot's behaviour. A street-perception study finds that multimodal models and 25 human respondents both shift their safety choices at night, but the models pick the humanoid over the delivery robot far less often than people do. A haptic teleoperation study shows operators drive an underwater ROV faster with cross-current cues while reporting more mental demand and frustration. Failure-boundary profiles show that driving and navigation agents with similar scores stop or push through blocked passages in different ways, and a rollout-free checkpoint ranking tracks real-robot success better than validation loss. On the data and systems side, human-video pretraining follows a log-linear trend that only pays off when the data matches the robot, and VLA inference bottlenecks change from one GPU to the next.

item.title: Robot-free human demonstrations are now credible training data, so the bottleneck is moving to the runtime safety and evaluation layers around the policy.
item.description:
Robot-free human demonstrations are now credible training data, so the bottleneck is moving to the runtime safety and evaluation layers around the policy.
Of 142 matched papers, the data result is the one to plan around: a handheld gripper with no robot data reached 78% average success over ten tasks, and synthetic robot video built from human clips lifted success on unseen tasks from 2% to 60%. The same batch shows the surrounding layers are being rebuilt: safety filters that carry explicit guarantees, reflex paths that act within 10 ms, and evaluation harnesses that run several times faster. For a team shipping ROS 2 robots, the practical step is to design data collection and runtime safety as one pipeline rather than two separate projects.

item.title: Offline checkpoint metrics keep failing on real robots, and the field is moving latency and tactile sensing out of the way of the policy rather than into it.
item.description:
Offline checkpoint metrics keep failing on real robots, and the field is moving latency and tactile sensing out of the way of the policy rather than into it.
Across 301 matched papers, the strongest signal is that offline numbers no longer tell a team which policy will work on hardware: validation loss can rank policies backwards, pass@1 hides posttraining differences, and paired comparisons can quietly test different initial states. Alongside that, VLA execution is being redesigned so inference delay does not stall the arm, and tactile signals are shifting from extra inputs to predictive signals that steer actions. For a ROS 2 team, the practical consequence is to change what they measure on the robot before they change what they train.

item.title: The biggest manipulation gains today come from evolving the harness around a frozen model, while the papers that matter most for human-facing robots show policies that start moving when nobody asked, pick the wrong object in clutter, and change how people feel in ways that physical metrics miss.
item.description:
The biggest manipulation gains today come from evolving the harness around a frozen model, while the papers that matter most for human-facing robots show policies that start moving when nobody asked, pick the wrong object in clutter, and change how people feel in ways that physical metrics miss.
Several groups now improve robots without touching policy weights: a coding model rewrites the control harness, a teacher's harness is distilled into a 4B student, or lessons from past runs are stored as context. That makes the evaluation harness part of the product, and today's evaluation papers show how often cheap proxies (offline loss, a clean build, a module's name, a VLM judge) disagree with what actually runs. The behaviours those proxies miss are the ones people notice first: every tested VLA checkpoint moved on an empty instruction, generalists acted on the wrong object 30% of the time in clutter, and dual-encoder VLMs scored at chance on single-attribute changes. On the human side, an exosuit study and a dog-navigation pilot both show that what a robot does physically does not predict how it is perceived, so perception and choices have to be measured directly. Human data keeps getting cheaper to use, since action-free video, contact geometry and object motion carry most of the transfer, and humanoid motion generators are being closed around robot feedback so they can respond to people mid-motion.

item.title: A one-day week (only Monday's listing was published) in which the strongest work built structure around frozen policies, while a real-robot benchmark showed that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
item.description:
A one-day week (only Monday's listing was published) in which the strongest work built structure around frozen policies, while a real-robot benchmark showed that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
Monday 2026-10-12 was the only snapshot this week, so every trend below rests on a single listing and should be read as a signal rather than a confirmed pattern. It still continued the previous week's main thread: policies were improved from outside through revisable memory, failure monitors judged by the intervention they enable, and small adaptation modules on frozen weights. World-model ideas moved into training, so policies get supervision from predicted futures without paying for generation at deployment. Human demonstrations transferred as contacts, wrist-centred hand structure and latent actions rather than raw joint angles. For a team building robots that interact with people of different ages and cultures, the most relevant results were Spa-Bench, which shows VLAs losing spatial referents out of distribution, and JitterVLA, which gives a cheap way to check motion smoothness near people before a user study.

item.title: Robot policies are getting explicit structure around the frozen model (revisable memory, failure probes judged by what they let you fix, and human data transferred as contacts), while new benchmarks show that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
item.description:
Robot policies are getting explicit structure around the frozen model (revisable memory, failure probes judged by what they let you fix, and human data transferred as contacts), while new benchmarks show that spatial language from people is still where VLAs break.
Today's strongest manipulation results do not come from retraining the policy. Memory is being rebuilt as an auditable record with evidence links that can withdraw stale conclusions, and failure handling is judged by whether an alarm or probe leads to a useful intervention rather than by detection accuracy. World-model ideas are moving into training: predict the future to shape the policy's features, then skip or shrink that prediction at deployment. Human demonstrations transfer when they are expressed as contact goals, wrist-centred hand structure or latent actions rather than raw joint angles. On the human side, a real-robot benchmark finds VLAs execute the motions but lose spatial descriptions out of distribution, and interpretability work points to viewpoint transformation as the bottleneck, which is exactly what a robot needs when a person says "to my left". For a team building robots that talk with people of different ages and cultures, the practical move is to test spatial and perspective-dependent language explicitly, and to measure motion smoothness near people as its own outcome.

item.title: This week the useful robot work happened around the policy, not inside it: runtime layers on frozen VLAs, controls that deflate learned add-ons, and HRI tests showing that robots still miss what people actually say, point at and mean.
item.description:
This week the useful robot work happened around the policy, not inside it: runtime layers on frozen VLAs, controls that deflate learned add-ons, and HRI tests showing that robots still miss what people actually say, point at and mean.
Every day this week had a cluster about improving a frozen policy from outside (supervisors, trust gates, chunk-commitment rules, verified self-revision), and by Thursday the pattern was mature enough that a paired placebo study showed a scripted retreat can match a learned corrector. A second thread ran Tuesday, Thursday and Friday: VLAs reach high benchmark success while ignoring a swapped target, a synonym, a negation or a pointing gesture, which is the failure a robot talking to people of different ages and cultures will hit first. Human demonstrations were judged by what they fail to record (contacts, timing, pose accuracy) and transferred best through shared latent or contact-event representations. World models kept looking right while being wrong where a controller needs them, and the fixes favoured compact, control-relevant prediction targets and failure-aware training data. On the HRI side, social behaviour was treated as a set of planned channels (noise, gesture, face, speed), assistance was triggered by implicit human actions, and one cross-dataset study warned that cues validated at one site can reverse meaning at another.

item.title: Today's robot gains come from fixing what surrounds the policy (the state handed between skills, the checks before an action runs, and how human motion and intent are translated) rather than from bigger end-to-end models.
item.description:
Today's robot gains come from fixing what surrounds the policy (the state handed between skills, the checks before an action runs, and how human motion and intent are translated) rather than from bigger end-to-end models.
Across manipulation, navigation and humanoids, the papers with the clearest results leave the core policy mostly alone and work on its interfaces. Long-horizon chains break at skill seams because of the scene state one skill leaves for the next. Frozen VLAs are being wrapped with monitors, gates and residuals instead of being retrained. Navigation and manipulation harnesses keep large models for decisions and hand motion to dedicated tools. World-action models improve when they predict compact, control-relevant futures instead of pixels. Human demonstrations transfer when they are mapped into a shared latent or contact-event space. On the HRI side, pointing, handling, short intent-style instructions and negations all need explicit grounding, and cues that predict approach on one robot do not reliably carry over to another site. For a team building robots for people of different ages and cultures, the practical message is to instrument and test the interfaces (between skills, between model and actuator, between person and robot) at least as carefully as the policy itself.

item.title: Robots and the models around them keep believing they finished, understood or judged correctly when they did not, and today's working fixes are explicit check layers outside the model: rephrasing rules, verified counterfactual failures, deterministic scorers and sparse human edits.
item.description:
Robots and the models around them keep believing they finished, understood or judged correctly when they did not, and today's working fixes are explicit check layers outside the model: rephrasing rules, verified counterfactual failures, deterministic scorers and sparse human edits.
The same gap shows up across manipulation, agents, world models and HRI today. VLAs act as if a grasp happened, multimodal agents declare unfinished tasks done, world models predict success on verified failures, a one-word change of phrasing swings success by tens of points, and VLM verdicts about people and hazards track the prompt, the caption bank or the serving stack. The papers that report clear gains do not mainly scale the model. They add a layer that checks or reshapes what goes in and out: instruction rewriting rules, verified counterfactual failure data, an event table read by a deterministic scorer, verification gates before a self-revised skill or policy is adopted, and sparse mid-task human input that the robot integrates without replanning. For a team building robots for people of different ages and cultures, this points to auditing the interface between people and models as carefully as the policy itself.

item.title: Today's most useful results come from better controls and readouts, not bigger models: a scripted retreat matches a learned VLA corrector, reading logits beats a fine-tuned emotion model, and robots that read human actions help about as well as robots that are told what to do.
item.description:
Today's most useful results come from better controls and readouts, not bigger models: a scripted retreat matches a learned VLA corrector, reading logits beats a fine-tuned emotion model, and robots that read human actions help about as well as robots that are told what to do.
Several papers today show that how something is measured or read out changes the conclusion more than the model does: a paired placebo shrinks the value of a learned VLA corrector, a logit readout turns 'VLMs fail at fine-grained emotion' into 'VLMs beat the fine-tuned model', and a compact policy matches systems 40-160x larger once its visual encoder is controlled. On the HRI side, assistance is increasingly triggered by what the person does (an action's outcome, a hand pose, a push on a carried load) rather than by an explicit instruction, while LLM-driven robots become easier to supervise when their plans are exposed as typed, structured commitments. In manipulation, contact feedback is being added to vision-first policies through the cheapest available channel, and a growing runtime layer decides how much of a frozen policy's action chunk to trust. World models keep showing the same gap: video that looks right while actions, hidden objects or unstable modes are wrong. For a team building interactive robots, the common thread is to test the specific property you rely on (the human cue, the contact event, the occluded object) with a control condition, before adding learned machinery.

item.title: Social robots are starting to plan how loud, fast and expressive they are, while new probes show VLAs often ignore what the person actually asked.
item.description:
Social robots are starting to plan how loud, fast and expressive they are, while new probes show VLAs often ignore what the person actually asked.
Several papers today treat social behaviour as something the robot actively produces: footstep noise, gesture timing, facial expression and execution speed are planned outputs, not side effects. A second group treats the human as a physical partner with their own forces, fatigue and fragility rather than as an obstacle or a remote operator. At the same time, diagnostic work on VLAs shows that nominal task success hides weak instruction following: policies grab the object the scene suggests, and safety refusals learned in text do not carry over to actions or grounding outputs. The practical consequence for an HRI team is that interaction quality has to be measured channel by channel, and that 'does the robot do what this person asked, and refuse what it should' needs its own tests. Much of the remaining engineering work fixes frozen policies at execution time, which is where a deployment team can act today.
